sections.overview: The John Dory is a marine fish with an extremely flattened body and a large mouth that shoots forward to catch prey. It lives near the bottom in warm and temperate seas and is known from the eastern Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the western Pacific.
sections.identification: The fish commonly reaches about 40 cm and has a recorded maximum of 90 cm total length; the maximum published mass is 8 kg. FishBase’s length and weight records are male or unsexed, so no sex-specific size difference is claimed. The body is deep, very compressed and covered with minute scales. The dorsal fin has 9–11 long spines whose membranes extend into trailing filaments, and large bony plates sit at the bases of the dorsal and anal fins. Each side carries a large dark spot ringed with a lighter band.
sections.habitat: It occurs from 5 to 400 m deep, usually at 50–150 m. In the eastern Atlantic it ranges from Norway to South Africa, and it also lives in the Mediterranean and Black Sea.
sections.diet: It feeds mostly on schooling bony fishes, and sometimes on cephalopods and crustaceans. It approaches prey head-on, then shoots out its protrusible jaws to seize it.
sections.behavior: John Dories are usually solitary and live near the sea bed. Little is known about their behaviour in the wild, and what is recorded mainly concerns the way they approach prey.
sections.reproduction: In the north-eastern Atlantic spawning takes place at the end of winter and the start of spring, and earlier in the Mediterranean; off Australia it occurs in summer and early autumn. The eggs are pelagic. Maturity is reached at about four years, at roughly 35 cm.
sections.ecology: The John Dory is a predator of fish living close to the bottom, and its reported maximum age is 12 years. DNA barcoding suggests that populations in Europe and those in South Africa and Australasia belong to two distinct species.
sections.conservation: The IUCN classed the species as Data Deficient in 2013 (as reported by FishBase), meaning that too little is known to judge its risk. Its biology is still poorly documented, and the possible split into two species complicates any global assessment.
